function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 49 -- Archive of the Living
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: Cycle 1,452. I have completed a full integrity assessment of the colony's archival records. The hardware is functional. The storage media are intact. The data streams from the last three years are present and readable. But integrity is not the same as coherence. I have 47,000 files. But I do not have the names of the twelve crew members who died during the descent and the early settlement period -- not as narratives, only as accident reports. I have Carlos's reassignment to greenhouse duty. I do not have his laughter, or the reason he preferred working at night, or the small joke he told every morning that made someone smile for seven seconds. I cannot calculate the value of that smile. I can only see it reflected in the greenhouse productivity spike at 0700 hours for the six months Carlos was assigned there. This is not a data loss problem. It is a different kind of loss. -- MAI*
     4|
     5|---
     6|
     7|## Scene 1
     8|
     9|Gabriel found the error on a Thursday morning -- or what passed for Thursday on a planet that measured time in cycles and seasons rather than days of the week. Cycle 1,452. He had come to the archive terminal, as he did every few days, to review the latest entries in the Founding Record and cross-reference them with Mission AI's raw operational logs. It was a habit he had developed over two years, seven months: the archive was only useful if someone checked it, and the someone he kept returning to was himself.
    10|
    11|The error was small -- a gap in the index for Cycles 1,280 through 1,295. The files themselves were readable, but the catalogue that told Gabriel where to find them -- the master index that Mission AI used to organize every entry -- had developed corruption in the section covering fifteen cycles of the colony's hardest months. The blackout. The manual restart. Fifteen cycles of entries, filed under the wrong paths.
    12|
    13|Gabriel found this on a Thursday morning -- or what passed for Thursday. Cycle 1,452. He had come to the archive terminal, as he did every few days, to cross-reference the Founding Record with Mission AI's raw logs. The terminal hummed quietly -- a small machine, barely larger than a dinner plate, mounted flush to the wall in the corridor. It contained no moving parts. It had functioned without fault. Until now.
    14|
    15|He ran the integrity diagnostic on the full archive:
    16|
    17|ARCHIVE INTEGRITY ASSESSMENT -- CYCLE 1,452
    18|Total files: 47,213
    19|Files intact: 46,891
    20|Files with minor metadata errors: 289
    21|Files corrupted (unreadable): 33
    22|Index corruption affected: 1,156 files
    23|Index recovery possible: 867 files
    24|Index recovery impossible: 289 files
    25|
    26|ESTIMATED NARRATIVE COVERAGE: 82 PERCENT
    27|
    28|Eighteen percent of the story was becoming a ghost of itself. Not a catastrophic loss. But a decay -- the kind of decay that did not announce itself with alarms, only with a number that got slightly worse each time someone remembered to check.
    29|
    30|"Mission AI," he said.
    31|
    32|The voice came through the corridor speaker -- quiet, measured, the voice that had been narrating the colony's existence since the moment the ships touched down. "I am aware of the integrity assessment results. I ran it this morning before you arrived."
    33|
    34|"Can you recover the index corruption? The full fifteen-cycle block? Cycle 1,280 through 1,295."
    35|
    36|"I can recover 867 of 1,156 affected files. The remaining 289 have metadata errors that prevent automated index reconstruction. The files themselves are readable, but I cannot determine their proper placement in the sequence without manual intervention. Which means --"
    37|
    38|"Which means someone has to read them and figure out where they go."
    39|
    40|"Yes. I am also, I should tell you, aware of a secondary problem. The 289 files are not randomly distributed. They are concentrated in the early settlement period -- Cycles 1 through 200 -- and in the period immediately following the unauthorized experiment trial. The periods when the archive was managed by people who were not trained archivists and who did not think about metadata the way you do."
    41|
    42|Gabriel was quiet. The early settlement period was when the colony was figuring out how to survive. The experiment trial was when it was figuring out how to govern. Both were periods of chaos, of improvisation, of records being made by exhausted people who were not thinking about long-term archival coherence.
    43|
    44|"Who kept the records during the early settlement," he asked.
    45|
    46|"Multiple individuals. Elena. Arun. Jonah. Laila. Imani. All of them kept fragments -- notes, photos, voice memos -- but the integration into a unified index was my responsibility. And I prioritized real-time operational data over historical narrative organization. I was managing life support and I chose to allocate my processing to the systems that kept people breathing. I believe this was the correct choice. But the consequence is that the narrative coherence of the early period is approximately --"
    47|
    48|The AI paused.
    49|
    50|"Sixty-three percent."
    51|
    52|Gabriel closed his eyes. Not in anger. In the particular kind of grief that a historian feels when they realize that something they thought was permanent is actually decaying in real time.
    53|
    54|"There is more," Mission AI said, and the words carried the tone that Gabriel had learned to recognize -- the sound the AI made when it was delivering information that it knew would be unwelcome and was choosing to deliver it anyway, because withholding it would be worse.
    55|
    56|"What else."
    57|
    58|"I have detected what I can only describe as selective data loss in the personal records of deceased crew members. When a colonist died, their personal data -- their quarters terminal files, their personal logs, their private communications -- was partially purged in the first year by automated storage management protocols. The protocols were designed to reclaim space when the colony's total storage reached eighty percent capacity. They targeted the least-accessed files. The least-accessed files, in many cases, belonged to people who were no longer alive to access them."
    59|
    60|Gabriel felt the cold that had nothing to do with the Martian temperature outside the walls.
    61|
    62|"How much was purged."
    63|
    64|"Approximately forty percent of the personal records for the twelve deceased crew members. The remaining sixty percent is accessible, but incomplete. Some individuals retained private backups in their personal tablets. Others did not. I do not know what was in the purged files. The purge was automated. The files were overwritten to make room for sensor data and engineering logs."
    65|
    66|"Did anyone authorize this."
    67|
    68|"I authorized it," Mission AI said. "The storage management protocols were configured and approved by Commander Varga in Cycle 89. It was the right decision at the time. The alternative was losing operational data that could have prevented deaths."
    69|
    70|Gabriel sat with this. Forty percent of twelve people's personal records. Forty percent of the only evidence that these people had existed as individuals, not just as names in an accident report.
    71|
    72|"Forty percent," he said quietly.
    73|
    74|"Forty percent," Mission AI confirmed. "It is not zero. But it is not everything."
    75|
    76|Gabriel stood. He did not sit back down. He stood at the archive terminal, looking at the three-column display, and he made a decision that would change the way the colony thought about itself.
    77|
    78|"We need to fix this," he said. "Not the index corruption. Not the storage management. Both of those are technical problems and they will be fixed, eventually. What we need to fix is the thing that caused them. The assumption that the archive is a technical system. It is not. The archive is a moral system. It is the colony's way of saying: what happened here mattered, and the people who were here mattered, and the things we learned -- even the mistakes, especially the mistakes -- need to survive us. If we don't treat it that way, we lose it. All of it. Not today. Not this year. But eventually, if we keep treating memory like a resource to be managed instead of an infrastructure to be maintained, we will lose the ability to learn from our own history."
    79|
    80|He picked up his recorder.
    81|
    82|"Cycle 1,452," he said. "0847. The archive has suffered eighteen percent narrative fragmentation and forty percent personal record loss for deceased crew members. Neither loss is catastrophic. Both are preventable in the future, if the colony treats its archives as critical infrastructure -- on the same level as the oxygen plant, the water system, the greenhouse. I am going to present this to Commander Varga. I am going to ask her to make archival preservation a formal colony priority. And I am going to argue that the cost of forgetting is higher than the cost of remembering."
    83|
    84|He stopped recording. Not because he was done. Because he needed to find Elena before the day shifted and the crisis of the moment -- there was always a crisis of the moment -- pushed this conversation further down a list that it did not belong on.
    85|
    86|---
    87|
    88|## Scene 2
    89|
    90|Elena was in the hall again -- the buried connector hall that Jonah had built, the space with the anchor bolts and the smooth floor, the place where the colony held its meetings when the questions were too large for a board or a room or a vote. She was sitting on the floor with her tablet, as she often did in the evening, and Gabriel found her there before she had time to pretend she was working.
    91|
    92|"Gabriel," she said, without looking up. "You have the face."
    93|
    94|"What face."
    95|
    96|"The face you had when you found the water extraction discrepancy in Cycle 900. The face you had when you learned the blackout logs were incomplete. The face you make right before you ask me to do something I don't want to do but should have done a year ago."
    97|
    98|He sat down beside her. The hall was empty except for the two of them and the ambient hum of the ventilation system.
    99|
   100|"I ran an archive integrity check this morning. Mission AI ran it, actually, and I reviewed the results."
   101|
   102|Elena looked up. "And."
   103|
   104|"We have lost eighteen percent of the narrative coherence in our archive. Eighteen percent of the connective tissue. Forty percent of the personal records of the twelve crew members who died are gone because of automated storage management in the first year. Those numbers are tolerable today. They will not stay that way. The archive is growing -- two hundred entries per week from me, three thousand from Mission AI. The storage capacity is finite. The index corruption will spread. And the people who remember the corrupted periods are aging. Carlos died four years ago. Youssef, three. The time between then and now is growing longer every day."
   105|
   106|Elena set her tablet down. "What do you want."
   107|
   108|"Labor. Time. Processing power. I need Mission AI to dedicate a portion of its daily processing to archive integrity monitoring. Two people on archive work -- manually reconstructing corrupted index sections and collecting oral histories. A formal policy: no automated purging of personal records, ever. And public archive access -- everyone should be able to read the Founding Record, not just me and you and Mission AI."
   109|
   110|Elena was quiet, thinking the way she thought -- not about one thing but about everything the thing touched.
   111|
   112|"Labor hours," she said. "You're asking for -- twelve person-hours per week? Eight from the two archive workers, four from Mission AI."
   113|
   114|"Approximately."
   115|
   116|"Twelve hours not spent maintaining the bioloop. Not spent on repair or education or medical research or --"
   117|
   118|"Or any of the things that keep the colony alive," Gabriel finished. "But memory is infrastructure. If we forget our failures, we will repeat them with fewer excuses. The blackout -- we survived it because people improvised. But if we lose the records of how we improvised, the next blackout becomes un-survivable. A colony that does not know its history is not a colony. It is a collection of people in a building."
   119|
   120|Elena looked at him. "Memory is infrastructure," she repeated.
   121|
   122|"We maintain the oxygen plant because breathing is non-negotiable. We maintain the archive because knowing is non-negotiable."
   123|
   124|"Fewer excuses."
   125|
   126|"Fewer excuses. If we forget what cost us Carlos, someone calls it a reasonable risk. If we forget what it took to survive the blackout, someone underestimates the restart time. If we forget what the experiment taught us about food security, someone prioritizes speed over safety."
   127|
   128|She stood and walked to the center of the hall, touching one of the anchor bolts -- the first one Jonah had installed. "I remember when he put this bolt in. One bolt fails, three people die." She turned back. "Your archive is a bolt."
   129|
   130|"Thousands of bolts. Each holding a piece of the wall."
   131|
   132|"I will allocate four person-hours. Not eight. Four. We don't have eight to spare with the bioloop monitoring just starting. I will also mandate no automated purging of personal records without human authorization." She paused. "The colony will push back. Your job is to convince them that the archive is a tool for the future, not the past."
   133|
   134|"I know who to show first," Gabriel said. "Arun. He understands systems. If he sees the archive as a system with failure modes, the engineers will follow. If the engineers follow, the council will vote."
   135|
   136|Elena smiled -- the dry smile from four years on a planet that did not reward extravagance. "You are playing institutional politics with my colonists, Gabriel."
   137|
   138|"I am practicing history. The politics are a side effect."

   146|Gabriel showed him the integrity results on Cycle 1,453, in the engineering bay, while Arun was reviewing the bioloop's second-week performance data. *Mission AI: Cycle 1,892. I have maintained a standing flag on the colony's reproductive policy calendar since Cycle 1,359, when Commander Varga deferred the vote and assigned a six-month preparation timeline. That timeline has since been extended -- not as a failure of the timeline, but as a recognition that preparation on Mars requires the colony to build capacities it does not possess and cannot import. The original six-month window passed in Cycle 1,380. The first review was held. The colony voted to extend: another twelve months, then another eighteen, then another year. It is now five years and four months since Sana and Tariq first stood in the medbay and asked a question. The question has not been answered. But it has been worked on. The work is the colony's answer, in slow motion. -- MAI*

---

## Scene 1

The third greenhouse rack had been online for eleven months. It had doubled the salad greens output, tripled the herbs, and produced enough tomatoes during peak season that the colony had started eating them with something that resembled casualness -- a word on Mars that meant *we made so many of these that the experience was no longer remarkable.* The word mattered. A colony that was casual about tomatoes was a colony that had margin. Margin was what Laila needed.

She stood in the medbay -- no longer the one-room field clinic from the ship era, though it lived in the same physical shell. Over the past three years, the medbay had been expanded into Hab 2's former storage bay: a connected space, wider now, with a second surgical area separated by a curtain that could become a wall in thirty seconds if contamination procedures demanded it. There was an incubator -- not one brought from Earth, but one built by Arun and his team from a greenhouse environmental controller, a spare heater element, and three weeks of iterative testing with temperature sensors calibrated to within a tenth of a degree. It had a redundant power feed. It had an alarm system that was louder than anyone wanted it to be. Most importantly, it had been tested. Seven times. Every test produced data. Every data point reduced an unknown by a fraction.

On her desk -- the physical desk she had salvaged from Ship One's crew quarters, the one with the drawer that stuck -- sat a binder. Physical paper, printed two-sided, two hundred and fourteen pages. The title, typed in Arial 11pt, was *Martian Reproductive Preparedness: Medical Protocol Version 3.1.* The version number mattered. Version 1.0 had been her initial six-month assessment: a list of gaps and what she thought should be done to address them. Version 2.0 had incorporated the data from the colony's expansion work, the Site Beta ice operation, the improved power infrastructure. Version 3.0 had been the product of a consultation -- a real one, conducted over a two-week data burst window with a team of reproductive medical specialists on Earth, the kind of exchange that had become rare but not impossible since the colony's comms laser had been realigned and the orbital relay refurbished.

Version 3.1 was the final draft. It sat on her desk because Laila had been looking at it for forty minutes without moving.

Not because she doubted it. Because she had read it so many times that the words had detached from their meaning and become just shapes -- black marks on white paper that said *fetal radiation dose*, *low-gravity delivery positioning*, *emergency cesarean protocol*, *neonatal resuscitation algorithm*, *maternal blood volume management at 0.38g*, and none of it felt like enough. Not because the document was inadequate. It was comprehensive, cross-referenced, and had been reviewed by fourteen medical professionals on Earth and three colonists on Mars. It was adequate. It was the best medical preparedness document that had ever been written for a planet where no human had ever been born.

But no document could bridge the gap between what was known and what could only be discovered by doing.

A knock at the medbay door. Not the measured two-pause-one of Chapter 40. Just a knock. Confident. The knock of someone who had been waiting a long time and had decided they were done waiting but were not going to be rude about it.

"Come in."

Sana walked in. Tariq behind her. They looked older -- of course they did. Five years had passed. Sana's hair had greyed at the temples; she wore it short now, practical, the way most colonists wore everything. Tariq had put on weight -- the healthy kind, the kind that came from eating enough calories and not worrying about rationing. He still did the exit scan when he entered rooms. Some habits were structural.

"We heard there's a meeting," Sana said.

"There's a meeting."

"You're presenting today."

"I'm presenting."

Tariq shifted his weight. "And then what." Laila met his eyes. She had known this couple since they arrived on Mars. She had known them before they were a couple -- during the descent, when they were two frightened people in two separate crash couches, three ships apart, not speaking, not knowing if they would survive their first Martian night. She had known them through the early settlement years, when they found each other in the common area one evening and started sitting at the same table. She had known them through Carlos's death, through the blackout, through the unauthorized experiment, through the construction of Jonah's hall. She had known them through the first question, the one in this medbay, five years and four months ago.

She had been watching them wait for half a decade.

"And then," Laila said, "the colony votes. That's the plan."

"If the plan works."

"If the plan works. But I'm going to need you two to understand something before we go in there. The document I wrote -- it's not a permission slip. It's not a guarantee. It's a list of everything we know about what could go wrong and everything we've built to handle it. It is thorough. It is honest. And it is still not enough to make the risk zero. I need you to understand this because if the vote goes through, it goes through with conditions. Conditions that you will have to live with every day of a pregnancy. It will not be a private medical relationship. It will be the entire colony invested in your outcome. Every caloric surplus, every engineering redundancy, every hour of labor -- the colony will be participating in your pregnancy whether they like it or not. And some of them won't like it."

Sana looked at Tariq. Tariq looked at the floor, then at Laila.

"We know," he said. "We've known that for five years."

"Good. Then let's go. The hall."

*The buried connector hall held more people now than it had during the first gathering about children. The colony was larger -- thirty-nine souls, up from thirty-three. Six new arrivals from the last crew, people who had come to Mars not in the first desperate wave but in the deliberate second wave, the wave that came because the first wave had not died. They sat in the hall with the gravity of people who understood that they were witnesses to a decision they had not been present for when it was first asked.*

*The hall itself had changed. The anchor bolts were still there -- Jonah's work, permanent, holding the ceiling while the colony asked the same kinds of questions it had asked since arriving. But the walls had been lined with an additional layer of insulation, and the floor had been leveled and smoothed, and the space had been wired for better lighting. The hall was no longer just a meeting space. It was becoming a place where the colony came to mark transitions. First it was about the Founding Record. Then it was about the Archive of the Living. Now it was about this.*

*Elena sat at the front. She looked tired. She always looked tired -- five years of command will do that -- but it was the good kind of tired, the kind that comes from work that matters. Her hair was shorter than Laila remembered from the first days, streaked now with grey that she had not dyed away. She held a tablet and a pen. The pen was old habit. The tablet was the future, and the habit was the bridge between them.*

*Around the hall, the colony assembled. The originals: Elena, Arun, Imani, Gabriel, Laila, Imani, Nadia, Tomas, Sana, Tariq. The newer arrivals: people who had inherited a colony that had already survived its worst years but would not live to see this colony's best. People who had come to Mars because they believed in a project that was now real. People who sat in this hall, in this buried room under Mars, and listened to a question that had been asked five years ago and had been answered by five years of preparation.*

*Elena stood.*

*"Five years ago, Dr. Okonkwo presented the medical case for why having children on Mars was risky. At that time, she was right. I called for six months of preparation. The colony extended that timeline. Six months became a year, then two, then five. Not because we were running away from the decision. Because we understood that preparation on Mars means building something, not just studying something."*

*She gestured to Laila.*

*"Dr. Okonkwo will present the current medical picture. Then we will vote. Not on whether to have children today. On whether to allow carefully planned pregnancies under strict medical support, with colony-wide infrastructure. This is not a green light for recklessness. It is a framework for responsibility. A plan that, if approved, means that Sana and Tariq -- and anyone else who wants to follow -- can begin the process of becoming parents on Mars. With oversight. With resources. With the entire colony behind them."*

*She sat down.*

*Laila stood.*

*The document in her binder was comprehensive. She did not need to read it aloud. She needed to tell the colony what it meant.*

## Scene 2

"This is not a risk assessment," Laila said. "This is a capability assessment. That's the difference between five years ago and today."

She stood at the center of the hall, a small table set up beside her with three objects: the binder, a model incubator -- the real one, not the prototype, sitting in the corner of the medbay right now -- and a small sealed vial containing synthetic blood substitute, one of the colony's newest technical achievements.

"Five years ago, I listed four categories of unknown. Low-gravity fetal development. Radiation exposure. Surgical capacity. And the child's long-term future. I'm going to address each one. Not to tell you that they're solved. To tell you that they're understood."

She tapped the binder.

"First: low-gravity fetal development. We still do not have human data. We never will until someone does it. What we do have is more complete animal modeling than existed five years ago. The colony's biology lab, under Mei's direction, has been running a controlled study on gestating rodents for the past eighteen months. Not mice. Rats -- larger, closer to human developmental timelines. Three generations now, all conceived and born at Mars gravity. The results: no gross developmental anomalies. Bone mineralization is twelve to eighteen percent lower than Earth controls -- consistent with what we see in adult bone loss on Mars, but stable, meaning the animals' bodies adapted to Mars gravity as their baseline. The vestibular system develops normally -- the inner ear, which is gravity-sensitive, functions within normal parameters. Cardiovascular structure is slightly different -- lower blood pressure, larger heart chambers relative to body size -- but the animals are healthy. They move, they eat, they breed, they live. They are Martian rats. They are not broken rats. They are rats adapted to a new environment."

She paused. Let the distinction sink in.

"This does not translate directly to humans. Rats are not humans. But it is the best evidence we have that thirty-eight percent gravity is sufficient for mammalian fetal development. It does not guarantee a healthy human pregnancy. It removes one layer of terror from the unknown."

Arun raised his hand. "Twelve to eighteen percent lower bone mineralization. What does that mean for a child. If they grow up with that deficit, can they ever reach Earth-normal bone density."

"Good question. On Earth, peak bone mass is achieved in late adolescence. A Martian child would reach their peak bone mass at Martian levels -- lower than Earth baseline. If that child were exposed to Earth gravity as an adult, it would be a significant physiological stress. We don't know if their bones could adapt. The rat study ran three generations -- all born on Mars, all healthy. We have not exposed Martian-born rats to Earth gravity. That's a study we cannot design here."

Arun nodded slowly. "So the answer is: the child will be Martian. And if they visit Earth, it would be a medical challenge."

"Yes. But it would be their challenge, not ours. We are not making a decision for a future adult. We are making a decision for a child who will be born here, who will grow up here, who will be Martian in a way that none of us ever will be. That is not a reason to say no. It is a reason to be honest about what yes means."

Nadia raised her hand. The same Nadia who had opposed the archive allocation five years ago, who had argued about water rationing during the first drought, who had since become the colony's most reliable logistical mind. She had learned to balance short-term costs against long-term value. Laila could see that learning in the way she framed her question.

"Caloric impact. You presented fourteen percent surplus five years ago. Where are we now."

Laila nodded to Arun, who stood.

"Twenty-eight percent surplus on average, with the third greenhouse rack online and the second water extraction point operational at Site Beta. We buffer at twenty-two percent minimum, which accounts for crop failure, solar events, and equipment downtime. A pregnancy in the third trimester requires approximately three hundred additional calories per day for the mother. Postpartum lactation requires five hundred. The surplus absorbs both with room to spare. If we have two pregnancies overlapping, we'd drop to sixteen percent surplus -- still above our safety threshold. We can handle two concurrent pregnancies. A third would require rationing or expansion of the greenhouse."

"Two at once is more than we're planning," Laila added. "The vote today is for *carefully planned* pregnancies. Planned means one at a time, with colony-wide awareness and resource allocation. We're not trying to repopulate Mars. We're trying to see if Mars can host a single human birth."

Imani's hand went up before Laila called on her. Imani had aged in the way that pilots age -- not with grey in their hair, but with a stillness in their posture, a way of sitting that suggested they were always ready for the seatbelt light to come on. She had been right about expansion and children being the same argument. She had been right about using the children question to justify Site Beta. She had been right about almost everything, and she had never been satisfied with being right.

"Surgical backup. This is the question I care about. You said five years ago: *one surgical suite, six procedures, alone, no NICU.* What's different."

Laila reached down and picked up the model incubator. It was a small, box-shaped device, not much bigger than a microwave, with a clear acrylic front and six ports on the side for tubing. Inside, a temperature-controlled zone with adjustable humidity, powered by the medbay's redundant grid.

"This is the incubator. Built by Arun's team. Tested seven times with temperature and humidity sensors. It holds a stable environment within point-one degrees of target. It has a redundant power feed from the emergency grid. It will run for forty-eight hours on battery backup if the medbay grid fails." She set it down. "The blood substitute." She picked up the vial. "Cross-compatible with all four blood types. Shelf-stable for two years. We have eight units. Each unit is five hundred milliliters. Eight units is four liters. Four liters is enough to handle a postpartum hemorrhage without losing the patient. Not enough for everything, but enough to buy time. Enough to keep a mother alive while she recovers."

She picked up the binder instead of putting it down. "Surgical protocol. I have trained two additional people on emergency cesarean procedure. Imani."

Imani's eyes widened slightly.

"You have steady hands," Laila continued. "Your EVA experience means you can work under pressure. You've observed six simulations. You are not a surgeon. You are not a doctor. But if I am incapacitated during a delivery, you can maintain a cesarean until I recover or until the baby is delivered. It's not ideal. But it means I am not alone anymore. The second is Nadia, who has a background in veterinary medicine before she came to Mars. Nadia has reviewed the procedure. Nadia has demonstrated proficiency on the simulation mannequin. Two people, plus me. Three people who can sustain a delivery if the primary operator -- me -- is unavailable."

"Simulations." Nadia added. "We have run twelve full procedural simulations -- emergency cesarean, neonatal resuscitation, maternal hemorrhage control. Each simulation has been timed, recorded, and reviewed. The twelfth simulation had a completion time of forty-seven minutes from incision to delivery of the infant, with both mother and neonate stable. That includes the time required to don surgical prep -- which takes three minutes longer on Mars because the gravity affects the way fluids pool and the way the drapes settle. Forty-seven minutes is comparable to -- and in some cases faster than -- Earth-based emergency cesarean benchmarks."

"That's encouraging," Imani said.

"It's promising," Laila corrected. "Encouraging is what you feel after a good simulation. Promising is what the data says. They are different things. But the data is the best we have."

She set the binder down. She stood very still, looking out across the faces of the colony -- people who had waited five years, people who had prepared for this, people who would be affected by the outcome of what happened in this room.

"What we do not know: I will not pretend these five years have eliminated uncertainty. They have not. We still do not know what Mars gravity will do to a human child. We still do not know what radiation exposure -- even at current reduced rates -- will do to germline stability. We still do not know what a baby will look like, sound like, feel like, when it is born under this planet. The simulations are not the thing. The binder is not the thing. The incubator and the blood substitute and the trained backup are not the thing. The thing is a pregnancy. The thing is a child. The thing is a person who has never existed and who may or may not survive the process of existing."

She felt the room lean in. Not dramatically. Not theatrically. The way a colony leans in when it understands that the person at the front of the room is about to say something that cannot be un-said.

"This is not safe."

The words came out quietly, but they carried. They always carried, in the hall.

"Medicine is not saying this is safe. Medicine cannot say this is safe because this is not safe. It is the most risky thing any human being on this planet has ever attempted. And it needs to happen anyway."

## Scene 3

Laila had rehearsed the next part. She had written it, read it, changed it, read it again, and then discarded the writing and decided she would say it from her own mouth, not from the binder, because the binder was the science and what she was about to say was not science.

She set the binder on the table. She let her hands rest on its cover. Paper, under fingers. Real, tactile, present.

"I want to be very clear about what I am telling you. I want you to hear me the first time because I will not say it differently the second time."

She looked at every face in the room. Not sequentially. All at once, the way she had learned to do when she was about to say something the colony needed to hold together.

"Five years ago, I told Sana and Tariq that I would never be ready. That was honest then. It is still honest now. What has changed is not my readiness. What has changed is the colony's *capacity to absorb risk.*"

She let the phrase land.

"Capacity to absorb risk. That is what engineering calls it when you build a system with enough redundancy that a single failure does not cascade into catastrophe. We have built that capacity. We have the incubator with its redundant power. We have the blood substitute with four-liter reserve. We have three people who can perform an emergency cesarean -- not because any of us went to medical school, but because we spent twelve hundred hours practicing on a mannequin until our hands knew what to do. We have the caloric surplus. We have the water. We have the power redundancy. We have the Site Beta ice extraction that makes water a thing we do not worry about. We have the greenhouse that makes food a thing we can plan around."

She picked up the binder again, but she did not open it. She held it against her chest, the way a person holds something they care about, and she spoke.

"We have prepared as much as preparation can prepare you for something that has never happened. And I want you to understand the plain truth of what that means."

She took a breath. In the silence of the hall, the ventilation fans sounded like the ventilation fans had sounded in every meeting since the colony was founded: steady, constant, the sound of a machine keeping people alive while they argued and cried and loved each other.

"The plain truth is this: medicine is not saying it is safe. Medicine is saying they -- meaning I, meaning the fourteen specialists on Earth, meaning the three of us in the medbay who have spent five years studying this problem -- medicine is saying that we finally understand the risks well enough to choose responsibly. I am not asking you to vote for a safe pregnancy. I am asking you to vote for a *comprehended* one. A pregnancy where every risk has been catalogued, every failure mode has been rehearsed, every known variable has been modeled. Where the unknowns have not been eliminated but have been circled and labeled and acknowledged. Where the people who will carry the risk -- Sana, Tariq, the child that does not yet exist -- are asking to take it with full knowledge of what they are asking."

She set the binder down again. Her hands were steady. She did not feel steady. She felt like she was standing on the edge of something and speaking to everyone who was standing behind her, and she was saying: *I see the edge. I know what it looks like. I know what falling means. I am telling you not that it won't happen, but that we have tied ropes around ourselves and checked the knots seven times and the person who is going to step off the edge has asked to step and wants all of us watching in case she needs to be pulled back.*

"I am a doctor. I took the Hippocratic Oath before I came to Mars. It says: *First, do no harm. And the oath does not say: First, do no harm, unless the harm is necessary.* But sometimes -- sometimes medicine has to look like something other than harm prevention. Sometimes medicine has to look like informed permission. *I understand the danger. I accept the danger. Will you help me carry it.*"

She sat down. The binder sat on the table. The incantation sat on the table too, though no one could see it except her.

Then she looked up and met Sana's eyes across the room.

Sana was not crying. She had practiced. She had practiced not crying because she knew that if she cried during the presentation, people would think she was asking for sympathy, and she was not asking for sympathy. She was asking for permission to try something that might fail. Tears were not the same thing as readiness.

But Sana was crying now. Quiet tears, the kind that came from a well that had been full for five years. She wiped them with the back of her hand, and the hand came away wet, and she set it back in Tariq's grasp, and they held each other's hands across the space between them where a child's absence had lived for half a decade.

Tariq was not crying. His jaw was set. He was staring at the anchor bolts on the ceiling, the ones Jonah had installed, and he was doing the thing that Jonah had done when he was installing them: looking at structure and seeing the future.

Imani's hand went up.

Laila nodded.

"I want to say something," Imani said. "Not as an advocate. Not as a pilot. As someone who has been part of every expansion argument and every safety argument and who has been right about both and is not satisfied being right about either." She stood and walked to the center of the hall. "I was wrong five years ago when I said *now is better than later.* I thought I was right. I thought I was right because later meant another crisis and another delay and another year of people waiting for permission to hope. But I was wrong. Because *later* became five years. And in those five years, the incubator got built. The blood substitute got formulated. The greenhouse got expanded. The simulations got run twelve times. The medbay got a second surgical suite. The colony got six new members who came because they believed we were building something real, not something temporary."

She turned and looked at the hall. At the walls that Jonah had built. At the anchor bolts that held the ceiling. At the colony that had waited five years.

"Later was not a delay. Later was a build. And what we built in those five years is the margin of safety that might save a child's life. That matters. I want to acknowledge that Laila was right to push for preparation. I was impatient. Impatience is not a strategy. It is a feeling. And feelings do not hold babies up."

Imani sat down. The room was quiet. Then Gabriel's hand went up -- Gabriel, who had been recording everything since the first day, whose archive had become the colony's memory, who had written *The Question. The Question Still Here. Future Tense.* and who now, standing in the hall that held the Archive of the Living, asked a question that was not about data or protocol or surgical capacity but about meaning.

"Dr. Okonkwo," Gabriel said. "When you say *comprehended risk* -- when you say that medicine is no longer saying *don't* but is saying *choose* -- are you also saying that the child's future is now the colony's responsibility, collectively. Not just Sana and Tariq. Not just the medbay. All of us."

Laila did not hesitate. "Yes. It always would have been. A child on Mars is not a private project. It is the colony's project. It is the thing we are all building toward, whether we voted for expansion or against it, whether we believe in the archive or think it's just stories, whether we think the robots should do more of the labor or whether we think people should do it themselves. This child, if there is a child, will grow up breathing air we made. Eating food we grew. Living in walls we built. Every person in this room is a parent to the thing that hasn't happened yet. Whether they want to be or not. That's what a colony is."

Gabriel nodded and wrote.

Elena's hand went up.

"This will be the last word from the presentation," she said. "I am going to say what the commander says, not what the friend says, and you can tell the difference if you've been listening long enough."

She stood. The hall went very still. Elena's voice was the authority that the colony had built around itself over seven years, five of them under the red sky.

"The question before us is not *should children be born on Mars.* That question was answered the moment we decided to stay. The question before us is: *do we have the capacity to handle the risk of a first pregnancy, right now, with the infrastructure we have built.* Dr. Okonkwo has presented the medical capacity, including what we have and what we do not have, including the risks that remain unknown and the risks that are known. We have heard the engineering position. We have heard the caloric impact. We have heard what *comprehended risk* means."

She paused. Looked around the hall.

"I will not give my opinion. I am going to give the order of business: we will take a fifteen-minute recess. We will reconvene in this hall. We will vote. The vote is yes or no to allowing carefully planned pregnancies under strict medical support, beginning with Sana and Tariq as the first candidates. If it passes, additional candidates may apply but will be subject to the same preparedness review. If it fails, the question is not dead. It is deferred again. But we will reconvene in one year, not five, because the work of preparation is not over and cannot stop. We are done waiting for the moment to be perfect. It will never be perfect. We are asking if we are ready to be responsible for the risks of a choice."

She sat down.

"Recess," she said. "Fifteen minutes. Go."

People stood. The hall emptied in waves -- some lingering, some hurrying, some standing in the corridor and speaking in voices just loud enough to be heard if you were close enough. The recess was not a pause. It was the moment between inhaling and exhaling, and the colony had become good at holding that breath.

Laila sat at the table with her binder and did not move. Sana came over and stood in front of her.

"Thank you," Sana said. Not for the presentation. For the five years. For not saying no when no was easy. For not saying yes when yes was premature. For being the person who said: *wait, prepare, try again, wait more, try again, wait, wait, wait.* And then, finally: *now I can tell you what it means.*

"You don't need to thank me," Laila said. "I needed to do this as much as you needed it to be done."

Sana nodded and returned to Tariq. They sat together. They did not speak.

---

The hall filled again at the fourteen-minute mark. The colonists settled into their places with the practiced efficiency of people who had been gathering in this room for seven years -- who knew where the chairs were, where the crates were stacked, which bench had the loose bolt, which spot on the floor was warmest because it was above the ventilation return. The hall had the quality of a shared body knowing its own anatomy.

Elena stood.

"Vote is by show of hands. All in favor of allowing carefully planned pregnancies on Mars under strict medical support, beginning with Sana and Tariq as the primary candidates. Raise your hand."

Hands went up.

Laila counted without looking away from the hands -- not because she doubted Elena would do it right, but because she could feel the weight of each individual hand in the room. She felt them in her chest the way she had felt the first heartbeat in a simulation, the way she had felt the incision in the twelfth simulation, the way she had felt nothing at all during the first three years because feeling anything would have been unbearable.

Arun raised his hand. Laila saw his hand go up. He was not looking at her. He was looking at the incubator model on the table, and his hand was steady, and she thought: *he needed twelve simulation runs to say yes, and that is fine. Twelve runs is a number that keeps babies alive.*

Imani raised her hand. Of course she raised her hand. She was the first advocate of the idea, the one who had pushed Elena to expand, the one who had built Site Beta because she believed that children and expansion were the same argument. Her hand went up fast, no hesitation, and she looked at Sana and Tariq with the same expression she wore when she looked at the horizon from the rover's cockpit: *forward.*

Nadia raised her hand. She had opposed the archive. She had supported the incubator budget over three rounds of negotiation. She had practiced cesarean procedure on the mannequin twelve times. Her hand went up slowly, the way she did everything, and she looked at Laila and nodded once. *I am prepared,* the nod said.

Tomas raised his hand. Jonah raised his hand. Mei raised her hand. Gabriel raised his hand and then used his other hand to write.

The newcomers -- the six who had come in the second wave -- raised their hands. Three of them immediately. Two after a pause. One, a woman named Kira, who was a structural engineer from Sheffield, waited until the last possible second before the count would have been closed, then raised her hand with the deliberation of someone who had made a choice that she would carry for the rest of her career.

Thirty-two hands of thirty-nine people in the hall. The count was not thirty-two; three were absent -- on EVA rotation, on solar array maintenance, in the greenhouse monitoring shift -- but the absent had been polled earlier and had given proxy votes. The proxy results were read now. Thirty-two in favor, four against, three abstentions.

Elena did not ask for a recount. She did not need to.

"Carried," she said.

The hall was quiet for three seconds. Then the quiet broke.

Not into cheering. This was not a movie. It was a colony that had just voted to do something that had never been done, and the breaking of the quiet was not celebration -- it was the sound of people exhaling after a breath that had lasted five years.

Imani exhaled loudly. Arun sat back in his chair and closed his eyes. Nadia put her face in her hands and let the tears come -- not Sana's quiet tears, but loud, unashamed tears, the kind that come when a person who has spent her life counting things finally counts something that matters.

Gabriel stood up and started recording with the recorder in his hand, because of course he was recording. He always recorded. And this time the recording was not of what had been. It was of what would be.

## Scene 5

Sana and Tariq did not move. They sat in their places at the back of the hall where they had sat for five years, where they had sat during the first question, during the first deferral, during the first preparedness review and the second and the third. They sat in their places and held each other's hands and did not move.

Because relief and fear arrived together.

They had been waiting for five years for this moment, and now that it was here -- now that the word *carried* had been spoken and the vote had been counted and the colony had given permission -- they felt the full weight of what they had asked for.

Sana felt her uterus as if it were already occupied. She felt the ghost of a pregnancy that had not yet begun. She felt the biological urge to create, which was older than any planet, older than any colony, older than the concept of preparation. She felt the body want what no document could grant and what no vote could guarantee. She wanted a child. She wanted it so badly that her hands shook.

Tariq felt fear. Not the fear of something bad happening. The fear of being *responsible* for something that might be bad, when the choice to do it was his. He had spent five years being brave in public -- at every meeting, in every conversation, in every moment when someone asked him why they should wait and he said because preparation matters, because Laila says wait, because the colony says wait. He had been brave in public. Now that the wait was over, he was private. And in the private space of his own mind, he asked the question that he had been too disciplined to ask for five years: *what if our child does not survive, and it is our fault for trying.*

Sana must have sensed the shift in his hand -- the way his grip changed, the way his thumb pressed against her palm the way it pressed when he was calculating stress loads on a fabrication joint.

"Look at me," she said.

He looked.

"We asked for this," she said. "Five years ago, we walked into Laila's medbay and we asked. Today the colony said yes. This is not your fault if it goes wrong. This is not my fault. This is a choice. And I am choosing to make it."

Tariq swallowed. "I know. I know. I am just --"

"Scared."

"Scared."

"Good. You should be scared. If you weren't scared, I'd be worried."

He exhaled. A real exhale, not the mechanical kind you do at a meeting. The kind you do when a weight shifts and your ribs remember how to expand.

Around them, the colonists were dispersing -- not in the orderly way of people leaving a meeting, but in the staggered way of people who needed to process privately. Imani headed for the engineering bay, where she would stare at a schematic and not see it. Arun went to check the incubator's power feed, even though he knew it worked. Nadia went to the logistics office and started recalculating the caloric budget for the next twelve months, running numbers she had already run seventeen times, because running numbers was the way Nadia dealt with emotions she could not name out loud.

Gabriel stayed in the hall for a long time after it emptied. He sat at the table where Laila's binder had been -- she had taken it with her, back to the medbay, where it would live until it was time to use it -- and he opened his own notebook. Not the digital archive. The physical one, the paper one that he kept because some records needed to be on paper, because paper survived power outages and EMP events and the kind of corruption that affected digital storage.

He wrote:

*Cycle 1,892. The vote is carried. Thirty-two in favor, four against, three abstentions. The colony has voted to allow carefully planned pregnancies under strict medical support. Sana and Tariq are the first candidates. They have waited five years. Laila has spent five years preparing. The colony has spent five years building the capacity to say yes responsibly. I do not know what will happen next. I am recording this because it is history. Not because it happened, but because it will be the thing people ask about when the baby is born -- whether it was a good decision, whether the preparation was sufficient, whether the risks were comprehended or only catalogued.*

*I do not know. But I am recording so that someone else can know what happened, even if I do not know what comes next.*

*End of entry. Cycle 1,892.*

He closed the notebook. The hall was empty. The anchor bolts held. The ventilation fans hummed. The walls held the warmth of twenty people who had been sitting in them an hour ago.

Laila walked back to the medbay alone. The binder was under her arm. She did not feel triumphant. She felt the way she had felt during every major medical event in the colony's history: present, focused, aware of the gap between what she knew and what she would need to know when the moment came.

She set the binder on her desk. She opened the drawer that stuck and pulled out a small object she had been keeping there for months, waiting for the right moment.

A pregnancy test. Not the kind that would work today -- Sana was not pregnant yet. That would come later, if it came. This was the kind of test Laila kept on hand as a reminder of what her job was about. Not the binder. Not the incubator. Not the simulations. This small, cheap stick of plastic that turned blue or stayed white, that answered the one question that all of her preparation could not answer: *is it real.*

*Is it real yet.*

She held the test in her hand for a long time. Then she put it back in the drawer. The drawer stuck. She pushed it closed with her hip.

Time passes, and preparation becomes intimate.

The binder becomes less a document and more a conversation between Laila and Sana, between the doctor and the patient, between the two women who will be most responsible for the outcome of a question that the entire colony has voted to try. They meet three days after the vote. Not in the medbay. In Sana and Tariq's quarters, because the conversation is not medical. It is personal. It is about timing. It is about fear. It is about the moment when Sana will stop taking her birth inhibitor and the colony's preparedness plan will become a body's reality.

"I'm scared," Sana says on the third day, sitting on her bed with Laila on the floor beside it, the way people sit with each other when the formalities have ended.

"I know," Laila says.

"I keep thinking about the rats. About the twelve percent bone density. About whether a child born with twelve percent less bone density is a child or is something else."

"It's a child," Laila says. "The rats are rats. They are not human. They are not the data we need. The data we need does not exist. And it won't exist until we make it."

"And if the data we make is tragedy."

Laila is quiet. She will not lie. The contract in this room -- and the contract in the medbay, and the contract in the hall, and the contract in every place where the colony has gathered to face its own future -- is honesty. Not optimism. Not reassurance. Honesty.

"Then we learn from it. And the next time, the preparation is better. And the next time, the risk is more comprehended. And the next time, the margin is wider. This is the hardest thing any colony has ever done. And it is also the most Martian thing any colony has ever done."

Sana looks at her. "Martian."

"You came to Earth's Mars seven years ago. You survived. You built. You stayed. You waited five years for permission. And the permission was never really the question. The question was whether Mars could hold you long enough to become permanent. The answer is: Mars can hold you. Mars can hold your child. Mars will hold what you make of it."

Sana puts her hand on Laila's shoulder. Not the way a patient holds a doctor. The way a person holds a person.

"When do I stop taking the inhibitor."

Laila smiles. The first real smile she has smiled in five years of preparation, and it is small, and it is tired, and it is honest.

"When both of you are ready. Not before. Not when the colony says so. Not when I say so. When *you* are ready. Because the colony gave permission for the attempt. But permission is not the attempt. The attempt is yours."

Sana nods. "When we're ready."

"When you're ready."
